1F (Linear Algebra)

Words: 254 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 254
1F OurBigBook.com
A basis of a vector space V is a family of vectors that is both linearly independent and a spanning set of V.
Write the given finite basis as B={v1​,…,vn​}. First, any other basis B′ must also be finite. Each vi​ is a finite linear combination of elements of B′, so the union S of the finitely many elements of B′ occurring in these n expressions is finite. Since S spans every vi​, it spans V. If some w∈B′∖S existed, then w would lie in the span of S, contradicting the linear independence of B′. Hence B′=S; write ∣B′∣=m.
It remains to prove the elementary Steinitz exchange lemma directly. If independent vectors w1​,…,wr​ lie in the span of v1​,…,vn​, express w1​ in terms of the vi​. Some coefficient is nonzero, so the corresponding vi​ can be solved for in terms of w1​ and the other vi​; replacing it by w1​ preserves the span. Inductively, after replacing k of the vi​ by w1​,…,wk​, the expression for wk+1​ must have a nonzero coefficient on one of the unreplaced vi​, since otherwise wk+1​ would be a linear combination of w1​,…,wk​. That vi​ can again be replaced. There are only n original vectors to replace, so r≤n.
Apply this argument first to the independent family B′ and the spanning family B to obtain m≤n, and then with the two bases interchanged to obtain n≤m. Therefore
∣B′∣=∣B∣​.
(1)

5C (Fluid Dynamics)

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 120
5C OurBigBook.com
Take x down the plane and y normally away from it, with the solid at y=0 and the free surface at y=h. A steady unidirectional falling film flow has velocity u=u(y)ex​. The streamwise Navier-Stokes equation reduces to
νu′′=−gsinα,
(19)
where ν is the kinematic viscosity. The lower no-slip boundary condition and upper stress-free boundary condition are
u(0)=0,u′(h)=0.
(20)
Integrating gives the velocity profile
u(y)=νgsinα​(hy−2y2​)​.
(21)
The volume flux per unit width is
Q=∫0h​u(y)dy=3νgh3sinα​​.
(22)
If the upper surface is replaced by a stationary solid plane, the second boundary condition becomes u(h)=0. The resulting plane-channel profile and flux are
u(y)=2νgsinα​y(h−y),Qclosed​=12νgh3sinα​=41​Q​.
(23)
The free surface exerts no tangential shear stress, whereas the stationary upper wall enforces no slip and exerts a retarding shear. This additional drag accounts for the reduced flux.

For distinct interpolation nodes x0​,…,xm​, define the degree-m divided difference by
f[x0​,…,xm​]=∑j=0m​∏0≤k≤mk=j​​(xj​−xk​)f(xj​)​.
(24)
It is the leading coefficient of the unique degree-at-most-m interpolating polynomial through those data.
Define
pn​(x)=f[x0​]+∑m=1n​f[x0​,…,xm​]∏i=0m−1​(x−xi​).
(25)
The partial polynomial pm​ agrees with pm−1​ at x0​,…,xm−1​. Moreover, the explicit formula for the divided difference gives
f[x0​,…,xm​]=∏i=0m−1​(xm​−xi​)f(xm​)−pm−1​(xm​)​,
(26)
so pm​(xm​)=f(xm​). Induction shows that pn​(xj​)=f(xj​) for every j. By uniqueness of polynomial interpolation, this is the required Newton interpolation polynomial.
For the recursion, substitute the explicit formulas for f[x1​,…,xm​] and f[x0​,…,xm−1​]. For an interior index j, the coefficient of f(xj​) in their difference is
(xj​−xm​)∏1≤k≤m−1k=j​​(xj​−xk​)1​−(xj​−x0​)∏1≤k≤m−1k=j​​(xj​−xk​)1​=∏0≤k≤mk=j​​(xj​−xk​)xm​−x0​​.

0=f′(x∗)=f′(xn​)+f′′(xn​)(x∗−xn​)+21​f′′′(yn​)(x∗−xn​)2.

The group G is a nontrivial finite p-group, so the nontrivial center of a finite p-group gives Z(G)={e}. If Z(G)=G, then Z(G) is already a nontrivial proper normal subgroup, so G is not a simple group. If Z(G)=G, then G is abelian. By Cauchy's theorem for finite groups, it has a subgroup of order p; every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, and this subgroup is nontrivial and proper because ∣G∣=p4. Thus in every case
G is not simple​.
(49)

The Sylow theorems state that if ∣G∣=pam with p∤m, then:
  • G has a Sylow subgroup of order pa;
  • every p-subgroup is contained in a Sylow p-subgroup;
  • all Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate;
  • their number np​ satisfies np​∣m and np​≡1(modp).

Interchange the two primes if necessary so that p<q. By the Sylow theorems, the number nq​ of Sylow q-subgroups satisfies
nq​∣p2,nq​≡1(modq).
(50)
If nq​=1, then nq​ is p or p2. The first is impossible because 1<p<q. The second would imply
q∣p2−1=(p−1)(p+1).
(51)
Since q>p is prime, it cannot divide p−1, so it must divide p+1. But q>p then forces q=p+1, impossible because p and q are both odd. Therefore nq​=1. The unique Sylow q-subgroup is a nontrivial proper normal subgroup, and hence
G is not simple​.
(52)

A map f:A→Rm is differentiable at p∈A when there is a linear map Df(p):Rn→Rm such that
f(p+h)=f(p)+Df(p)h+r(h),∣h∣∣r(h)∣​⟶0.
(53)
The linear map Df(p) is the Frechet derivative of f at p.
The multivariable chain rule states that if f is differentiable at p and g is differentiable at f(p), then
D(g∘f)(p)=Dg(f(p))∘Df(p)​.
(54)
Indeed, write f(p+h)=f(p)+Ah+r(h) and g(f(p)+k)=g(f(p))+Bk+s(k), where r(h)=o(∣h∣) and s(k)=o(∣k∣). Since k=Ah+r(h)=O(∣h∣),
g(f(p+h))=g(f(p))+BAh+Br(h)+s(Ah+r(h)),
(55)
and the last two terms are o(∣h∣). This proves the formula.
For matrix inversion near the identity matrix,
(I+h)−1=I−h+h2(I+h)−1.
(56)
The last term is O(∥h∥2) because inversion is bounded near I. Therefore the inversion map is differentiable at I and
Df(I)(h)=−h​.
(57)

A metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space.
Let x(1),x(2),… be a Cauchy sequence in X, where x(j)=(x1(j)​,x2(j)​,…). For each positive integer N, choose JN​ such that
d(x(j),x(k))<2−N(j,k≥JN​).
(63)
This inequality says that the first N coordinates of x(j) and x(k) agree. Consequently each coordinate xn(j)​ is eventually constant. Let xn​ be its eventual value and put x=(x1​,x2​,…)∈X.
For j≥JN​, the first N coordinates of x(j) agree with those of x, so
d(x(j),x)<2−N.
(64)
As N is arbitrary, x(j)→x. Therefore
(X,d) is complete​.
(65)

ψ′′=[f′′−2yf′+(y2−1)f]e−y2/2,

and hence f obeys the Hermite differential equation
f′′−2yf′+(ϵ−1)f=0​.
(90)
If f is monic of degree N, the coefficient of yN in this equation is ϵ−1−2N. It must vanish, so
ϵ=2N+1,E=ℏω(N+21​)​.
(91)
Writing f=∑k=0N​ak​yk gives the recurrence
ak+2​=(k+2)(k+1)2(k−N)​ak​.
(92)
The coefficient of yN−1 first gives aN−1​=0, and the recurrence preserves parity. If N is even, every odd coefficient vanishes, so f is an even function. The Gaussian factor is also even; therefore the stationary state ψ has even parity.

Use E=−∇ϕ and Gauss's law ∇⋅E=ρ/ϵ0​. The divergence theorem and the decay at infinity give
∫ρϕdV=ϵ0​∫ϕ∇⋅EdV=ϵ0​∫∇⋅(ϕE)dV−ϵ0​∫E⋅∇ϕdV=ϵ0​∫∣E∣2dV.
(93)
Multiplying by 1/2 proves that the two expressions for the electrostatic energy agree.
The uniform volume charge density in the thick shell is
ρ0​=4π(b3−a3)3Q​.
(94)
Spherical symmetry and the integral form of Gauss's law give
E(r)=⎩⎨⎧​0,4πϵ0​Q​(b3−a3)r2r3−a3​r,4πϵ0​r2Q​r,​0≤r<a,a≤r≤b,r>b.​​
(95)
Thus ∣E∣ is zero inside, rises continuously through the charged region, reaches Q/(4πϵ0​b2) at b, and then decays as r−2. Taking ϕ(∞)=0 and integrating E=−dϕ/dr gives
ϕ(r)=⎩⎨⎧​ϕ(a),4πϵ0​Q​[b1​+b3−a3(b2−r2)/2+a3(1/b−1/r)​],4πϵ0​rQ​,​r<a,a≤r≤b,r>b.​
(96)
The electric potential is continuous, constant inside, decreases smoothly across the charge, and continues as 1/r outside.
As b→a, the charge becomes a surface shell. Then
E={0,Qr/(4πϵ0​r2),​r<a,r>a,​ϕ={Q/(4πϵ0​a),Q/(4πϵ0​r),​r≤a,r≥a.​
(97)
The potential remains continuous, but the normal electric field jumps by Q/(4πϵ0​a2) across the surface charge density.
The field-energy expression gives
U=2ϵ0​​∫a∞​(4πϵ0​r2Q​)2,4πr2dr=8πϵ0​aQ2​=21​Qϕ(a).
(98)
The charge-potential expression gives the same result directly because the entire charge lies where the potential equals ϕ(a):
U=21​∫ρϕdV=21​Qϕ(a).
(99)
This is the electrostatic energy of a uniformly charged spherical shell.
Since ϕ(a)=Q/(4πϵ0​a) is proportional to Q,
δU=δ(8πϵ0​aQ2​)=ϕ(a)δQ​
(100)
to first order. This is the work required to bring the additional charge δQ from infinity to the potential created by the charge already present.

17C (Fluid Dynamics)

Solution

Words: 198
17C OurBigBook.com
For an incompressible flow, ∇⋅u=0. If the flow is also irrotational, then locally u=∇ϕ for a velocity potential, and therefore
∇2ϕ=∇⋅u=0.
(101)
The boundary conditions are
∂r∂ϕ​​r=a​=0,∇ϕ⟶Uex​(r→∞),∫02π​∂θ∂ϕ​dθ=κ.
(102)
The fluid region is not simply connected, so a potential may change by the constant κ after one circuit while its gradient remains single-valued. Superposing uniform flow, the cylinder doublet, and the circulation gives the potential flow around a circular cylinder with circulation
ϕ(r,θ)=U(r+ra2​)cosθ+2πκ​θ​.
(103)
Its velocity components are
ur​=U(1−r2a2​)cosθ,uθ​=−U(1+r2a2​)sinθ+2πrκ​.
(104)
On r=a, ur​=0 and, with λ=κ/(4πUa),
uθ​=2U(λ−sinθ).
(105)
The Bernoulli equation gives p=p∞​+ρ(U2−uθ2​)/2. The pressure force per unit length on the cylinder is
F=−a∫02π​per​dθ=2ρa​∫02π​uθ2​(cosθex​+sinθey​)dθ.
(106)
The x component vanishes by symmetry, while ∫02π​sin2θdθ=π gives
F=−4πρaU2λey​=−ρκUey​​,
(107)
in agreement with the Kutta–Joukowski theorem.
A stagnation point satisfies ur​=uθ​=0. On the cylinder this means sinθ=λ. Thus ∣λ∣<1 gives two surface stagnation points, ∣λ∣=1 gives one coincident surface point, and ∣λ∣>1 gives none on the surface. Away from the cylinder, ur​=0 requires cosθ=0. Solving uθ​=0 then gives one physical exterior root when ∣λ∣>1:
r=a(∣λ∣+λ2−1​),θ={π/2,3π/2,​λ>1,λ<−1.​​
(108)
At ∣λ∣=1 this root lies on r=a and agrees with the single surface point.

For this Adams–Moulton method, the characteristic polynomials of a linear multistep method are
ρ(w)=w2−w,σ(w)=125w2+8w−1​.
(113)
Expansion at zero gives
ρ(ez)−zσ(ez)=−241​z4+O(z5).
(114)
Part (a) therefore shows that the method has order exactly three.
It is consistent because its order is at least one. The roots of ρ(w)=w(w−1) are 0 and 1; both lie in the closed unit disk, and the only unit-modulus root is simple. Thus the method is zero-stable. By the Dahlquist equivalence theorem, consistency and zero stability imply convergence. Hence the method is
third-order and convergent​.
(115)

The Neyman-Pearson lemma says that for simple hypotheses with densities f0​,f1​, a size-α test that rejects where f1​/f0​>k and accepts where f1​/f0​<k, with possible randomization on equality to attain size α, is most powerful among all tests of size at most α. To prove it, let φ∗ be this test and φ any competing test. Pointwise,
(φ∗−φ)(f1​−kf0​)≥0.
(116)
After integration,
E1​φ∗−E1​φ≥k(E0​φ∗−E0​φ)≥0,
(117)
which proves maximal power.
For the exponential sample, with S=∑i​Xi​=nX,
L(λ0​)L(λ1​)​=(λ0​λ1​​)nexp((λ0​−λ1​)S).
(118)
Since λ1​<λ0​, this ratio is increasing in S. The likelihood-ratio test therefore rejects for large X:
Rα​={X>cα​},1−Gn,λ0​​(ncα​)=α​,
(119)
where Gn,λ​ is the distribution function of the rate-parameterized Gamma distribution Γ(n,λ).

β(λ)=Pλ​(X>cα​)=1−Gn,λ​(ncα​)​.

A level-α test is uniformly most powerful for a composite alternative when its power is at least that of every other level-α test at every parameter value in that alternative.
For every fixed λ1​<λ0​, the likelihood ratio is increasing in the same statistic S, and the size-α threshold is always the null quantile ncα​, independent of λ1​. The Neyman-Pearson lemma therefore makes the test from part (a) most powerful against every individual λ1​<λ0​. Consequently it is
uniformly most powerful for H0​:λ=λ0​ against H1​:λ<λ0​​.
(121)

Let the common initial state be x and the robber's final state be y. Part (a) gives their joint distribution as
π(x)P∗(x,y)=π(y)P(y,x).
(125)
Let τy​=min{n≥0:Xn​=y} be the cop's hitting time of y when starting from x. For a chain started from y, condition on its first step to obtain
Ey​Ty+​=1+∑x​P(y,x)Ex​τy​.
(126)
Hence the expected catch time, averaged over the displayed joint law, is
∑x,y​π(y)P(y,x)Ex​τy​=∑y​π(y)(Ey​Ty+​−1).
(127)
Using Kac's lemma once more gives
E[catch time]=y∑​π(y)(π(y)1​−1)=N−1​.
(128)
The convention τy​=0 correctly counts an immediate catch when the robber's reverse step leaves it at the common starting state.
